description: Executable behavioural specification for the legacy COBOL account management system. This file is the single source of truth for migration parity: the same scenarios are replayed against the COBOL binary and against any modern port.

contract.summary: A scenario feeds a fixed list of stdin lines to a target program and captures stdout. Output is reduced to an ordered list of normalised 'facts'. A port proves equivalence by producing the same fact sequence.

facts.credited:<amount>: A credit completed and reported the resulting balance.
facts.debited:<amount>: A debit completed and reported the resulting balance.
facts.insufficient_funds: A debit was refused because the balance was too low.
facts.rejected: The input was refused by validation. Modern ports only - the legacy system has no validation.
facts.exit: The program printed its farewell and terminated.
facts.runaway: The program produced unbounded output and had to be killed. This is a defect, not a feature.
facts.session_end: Boundary between two separate process invocations in a multi-session scenario.

contract.amountNormalisation: Amounts are compared as unpadded fixed-point strings with exactly two decimals. COBOL prints '001200.00'; a modern port may print '1200.00' or '$1,200.00'. Both normalise to '1200.00'.

parityLevels.strict: Core business behaviour. A port MUST reproduce expectLegacy exactly. Deviating here is a regression.
parityLevels.quirk: A defect or accident of the COBOL implementation. A port may reproduce expectLegacy (bug-for-bug migration) or implement expectModern (deliberate remediation). Choose one policy and hold it; never drift silently.

contract.vocabulary: A port is free to change layout, colour and number formatting, but must keep the message keywords ('balance', 'credited', 'debited', 'Insufficient funds', 'Invalid choice') so a single shared normaliser can read both systems.

scenarios.title: View the opening balance
scenarios.notes: The account opens at 1000.00, hard-coded in data.cob.

scenarios.title: Balance is displayed zero-padded to six integer digits
scenarios.notes: The upstream README claims the program prints 'Current balance: 1000.00'. It actually prints '001000.00' because PIC 9(6)V99 is displayed unedited. Presentation-only, so a port should modernise it.

scenarios.title: Credit the account with a valid amount
Credit the account with zero
scenarios.notes: The legacy system reports 'Amount credited' for a zero-value transaction. An accounting system should refuse to record a no-op movement.

scenarios.title: Debit the account with a valid amount
Debit more than the available balance
scenarios.notes: The one guard the legacy system gets right.

scenarios.title: Debit the account with zero
Debit exactly the available balance
scenarios.notes: Boundary the original test plan never covered. The comparison is >=, so draining the account to zero is permitted.

scenarios.title: Debit one cent more than the available balance
scenarios.notes: Confirms the guard is inclusive on the correct side.

scenarios.title: Exit the application
Credit then debit in one session
Balance is retained across operations within one session
A negative credit is silently treated as a positive one
scenarios.notes: AMOUNT is PIC 9(6)V99 - unsigned. The minus sign is discarded, so '-100.00' credits 100.00.

scenarios.title: A negative debit is silently treated as a positive one
scenarios.notes: Same unsigned-field defect on the debit path.

scenarios.title: A non-numeric amount is silently treated as zero
scenarios.notes: No NUMERIC class test, so garbage becomes 0 and the program reports success.

scenarios.title: An amount longer than the field is truncated before it is parsed
scenarios.notes: ACCEPT fills the 8-byte field from the left: '12345678.99' becomes '12345678', which then overflows PIC 9(6)V99 down to 345678.00.

scenarios.title: A credit that overflows the balance field silently destroys money
scenarios.notes: 1000.00 + 999000.00 = 1000000.00, which does not fit PIC 9(6)V99. There is no ON SIZE ERROR clause, so the leading digit is discarded and the balance becomes 0.00. The program still reports the credit as successful.

scenarios.title: A third decimal place is truncated rather than rounded
scenarios.notes: 10.999 becomes 10.99. There is no ROUNDED clause and no input validation, so sub-cent value is silently discarded.

scenarios.title: End of input causes an unbounded menu loop
scenarios.notes: ACCEPT at end-of-file leaves the field unchanged and never signals EOF, so the menu loop spins forever emitting 'Invalid choice'. Redirecting the program from a file that lacks a trailing '4' fills the disk.

scenarios.title: A multi-digit menu choice is truncated to its first digit
scenarios.notes: USER-CHOICE is PIC 9 - one byte. Typing '12' silently selects option 1.

scenarios.title: An empty menu choice is rejected
scenarios.notes: The one input path where the legacy default-to-zero behaviour produces a sensible result.

scenarios.title: Scientific notation is not understood and becomes zero
The balance does not survive a restart
scenarios.notes: The balance lives in operations.cob's own FINAL-BALANCE in WORKING-STORAGE - process memory that survives CALLs but not the process. data.cob is entered but matches neither branch (finding L-10), so nothing is stored anywhere. Every restart silently reopens the account at 1000.00.

scenarios.title: Surrounding whitespace in an amount is tolerated
scenarios.notes: Documented so a port does not accidentally become stricter than the original on a harmless input.

scenarios.title: A sub-cent amount is silently discarded and reported as a successful credit
scenarios.notes: 0.005 becomes 0.00 in a PIC 9(6)V99 field. The transaction moves nothing and the program still reports 'Amount credited'. Truncation always favours the institution, which is the pattern auditors look for.

scenarios.title: An amount at the field's stated maximum still loses its last digit
scenarios.notes: 999999.99 is the largest value PIC 9(6)V99 can hold, yet it is 9 characters entering an 8-byte field. ACCEPT truncates it to '999999.9' = 999999.90 before the addition, which then overflows. Independent confirmation of the L-04 mechanism at the boundary where it is least expected.
